The Scent Atlas

Perfume from everywhere

Small perfume houses, attars and old scent rituals from around the world, explained in plain words, with prices in Canadian dollars.

Theme

Tap a country, then a city, a house, its signature scent and any single note. Tapping a note lights up every house in the world that uses it.

To move the map: drag with a mouse, use two fingers on a phone, or the + and − buttons. One finger scrolls the page. Pins are placed on each house's city; houses marked "country" have no exact city on record. Colours show each house's main style. Prices are as last checked; CAD figures are estimates. Not affiliated with any brand.

How to read a scent

Words you will meet

Same building blocks, different moods

Most modern perfumes share a handful of workhorse materials. For an exhibition, perfumer Naoko (@naoko_perfumer) made four scents meant to read as "cute", "elegant", "sexy" and "classic", each from 15 materials or fewer, and all four used the same six: bergamot (bright citrus), Hedione (airy jasmine glow), Iso E Super (soft, cedary 'skin' warmth), Ambroxan (warm, salty amber), and two musks, Habanolide and Romandolide (clean, cosy laundry-skin). What changes the mood is the few materials added on top and how much of each is used. So a scent's "gender" or personality comes from the recipe, not the ingredients themselves.

Scent traditions

Old ways of wearing scent around the world: incense, smoke baths, attars, garlands and flower waters. Each card says how easy it is to get from Canada, where to buy the raw material and which modern perfumes echo it. Tap one to see it on the map.
